channel.title: Juan W. Hong, Attorney at Law — Korean Law Guides for Foreign Nationals
channel.description: Plain-English guides to Korean law for foreign residents — immigration and visas, criminal defense, employment, real estate, family law, and tax.

item.title: Insurance Claim Denied in Korea? How Foreigners Can Fight Back
item.description: A Korean insurer refused to pay, citing nondisclosure or a policy clause? The 1-month/3-year rule, unexplained terms, the 3-year claim deadline, mediation.

item.title: Sick Leave in Korea: Is It Paid? Rights of Foreign Workers
item.description: Korean labor law gives no general paid sick days: your contract or company rules decide. When 산재 pays 70% instead, and when you cannot be fired.

item.title: Broken Engagement in Korea: Gifts, Damages and Who Pays
item.description: Korean law lets you end an engagement but never forces a wedding. When the other side owes damages (Civil Act Art. 806) and who keeps the gifts (예물).

item.title: Co-Signing a Loan in Korea (보증): What a Guarantor Owes
item.description: A guarantee (보증) in Korea is valid only if signed on paper — not by app or message. What a guarantor or joint guarantor (연대보증) owes, and the defences.

item.title: Korean Police Case After You Left Korea: Summons and Warrant
item.description: Back home and Korean police are calling? The case does not close: the limitation clock can stop while you are abroad, and a warrant can wait for your return.

item.title: Spouse’s Debt in Korea: Are You Liable? The Household Rule
item.description: In Korea you do not owe your spouse’s loans just because you are married. The exceptions: household debts (일상가사, Civil Act Art. 832) and what you signed.

item.title: Logged Into Someone’s Account in Korea? Hacking Charges
item.description: Checking a partner’s Instagram or a former employer’s drive with a password you knew can be “intrusion” in Korea: up to 5 years or ₩50M. What to do now.

item.title: Undeclared Goods at Korean Customs (관세법): Fines and Charges
item.description: Goods not declared at Incheon, or parcels imported to resell? Smuggling under Korea’s Customs Act means up to 5 years. How the customs notice and 15 days work.

item.title: Accused of a Sham Marriage in Korea (위장결혼): Visa and Charges
item.description: Immigration says your marriage is fake? A false marriage registration can mean up to 5 years, a cancelled F-6 visa and deportation. How genuine couples answer.

item.title: Police Search Warrant in Korea: Phone Seized? Your Rights Now
item.description: Korean police searched your home or took your phone? See the warrant, attend the data copying, get the seizure list and ask for it back. What to do today.

item.title: Caught in a Prostitution Case in Korea (성매매): Fine, Record, Visa
item.description: Paying for sex is a crime in Korea for both sides: up to 1 year or ₩3M. Under 19, far more. What usually follows a police stop, and what it means for your visa.

item.title: Accused of Rape in Korea (강간): Penalties and First Steps
item.description: Rape (강간) in Korea carries at least 3 years, and settlement no longer ends the case. Detention, the police interview, evidence and what it means for your visa.

item.title: Suing Your Spouse's Affair Partner in Korea (상간자 소송)
item.description: In Korea you can claim damages (위자료) from the person your spouse had an affair with, even without a divorce. The 3-year deadline, evidence and when it fails.

item.title: Accidentally Injured Someone in Korea? Negligent Injury (과실치상)
item.description: Hurting someone by accident in Korea can still be a crime: 과실치상 (fine up to ₩5M, ends if the victim objects) or 업무상과실치상 (up to 5 years). What to do now.

item.title: Paternity Suit in Korea (인지청구): When the Father Refuses
item.description: Korean father won't acknowledge your child? A paternity suit (인지청구) can make him: DNA test orders, child support, nationality, and the 2-year rule after death.

item.title: Marriage Annulment in Korea (혼인무효·취소): Grounds and Deadlines
item.description: Korea has two ways to undo a marriage: a void marriage (혼인무효) and annulment (혼인취소). Fraud must be raised within 3 months of finding out.

item.title: Sent Money to the Wrong Account in Korea? How to Get It Back
item.description: Typed the wrong account number in Korea? Call your bank, then use KDIC's mistaken-transfer return service (착오송금 반환지원), then court. Spending it is embezzlement.

item.title: Water Leak in a Korean Apartment: Who Pays, Landlord or Tenant?
item.description: A leak from upstairs or a burst pipe in a rented flat in Korea: what the landlord must fix (Civil Act Art. 623), what you must report, who pays the neighbor.

item.title: Property Division in a Korean Divorce (재산분할): 2-Year Limit
item.description: In a Korean divorce the family court divides what both spouses built (재산분할); the claim ends 2 years after divorce. Alimony (위자료) is a separate claim.

item.title: Minor Offense Tickets in Korea (경범죄): Pay in 10 Days or Court
item.description: Littering, public urination, a drunken scene, cutting the line, an unpaid taxi: Korea's Minor Offenses Act. Pay the ticket in 10 days or face a summary trial.

item.title: Self-Defense in Korea (정당방위): When Hitting Back Is Legal
item.description: Korea excuses defence against a present, unjust attack only if your response was reasonable (Criminal Act Art. 21). Why both sides are often charged.

item.title: Juvenile Cases in Korea (소년보호사건): If Your Child Is Accused
item.description: Under 19 in Korea, a case can go to the juvenile division instead of a criminal trial. Children aged 10 to 13 are never prosecuted. What parents should know.

item.title: Sending Sexual Messages in Korea (통신매체이용음란): Penalty
item.description: Sending sexual texts, photos or calls to someone in Korea is a sexual offence: up to 2 years or 20M won (Sexual Violence Punishment Act Art. 13).

item.title: Is It Legal to Record a Conversation in Korea? (녹음)
item.description: In Korea you may record a conversation you take part in. Recording other people's private talk is a crime: 1 to 10 years, with no fine option.

item.title: Lent Money in Korea and Not Repaid? How to Get It Back (대여금)
item.description: Lent money to a friend, partner or co-worker in Korea? Evidence, demand letter, 5% and 12% interest, the 10-year limit, and when not repaying is fraud.

item.title: Driving Without a License in Korea (무면허운전): 1 Year or ₩3M
item.description: An expired international permit, a foreign license alone or a suspended license all count as 무면허운전 in Korea: up to 1 year or 3M won (Art. 152).

item.title: Assaulting a Police Officer in Korea (공무집행방해): Up to 5 Years
item.description: Pushing, hitting or threatening an on-duty officer in Korea is 공무집행방해: up to 5 years or 10M won (Art. 136). The officer's forgiveness does not end it.

item.title: Property Damage in Korea (재물손괴): Up to 3 Years or 7M Won
item.description: Breaking, hiding or making someone's property useless on purpose is 재물손괴 in Korea: up to 3 years or 7M won (Art. 366). Accidents are civil, not criminal.

item.title: Trespassing in Korea (주거침입): Up to 3 Years, Even for Landlords
item.description: Entering a home, a managed building or someone's room without consent, or refusing to leave, is 주거침입 in Korea: up to 3 years or 5M won (Art. 319).

item.title: Bitten by a Dog in Korea: Owner Liability, Charges, Compensation
item.description: A dog bite in Korea: the owner pays damages unless they took proper care (Civil Act Art. 759), and an unleashed dog that injures someone can mean up to 2 years.

item.title: Cancel a Korean Lease After Paying 계약금: Lose It or Get Double
item.description: Paid the contract deposit (계약금) on a Korean lease and want out? You can walk away by giving it up; a landlord who backs out repays double (Civil Act Art. 565).

item.title: Forged Documents in Korea (문서위조): Visa Papers, IDs, Diplomas
item.description: Forging or using a fake document in Korea: up to 5 years (private) or 10 (public). In a visa file it is also an Immigration Act crime and a deportation ground.

item.title: Stolen Goods in Korea (장물죄): Up to 7 Years for Buying or Keeping
item.description: Buying, keeping, carrying or selling goods you know are stolen is 장물 in Korea: up to 7 years or 15M won (Criminal Act Art. 362). Dealers: negligence counts.

item.title: Deepfake Sexual Images in Korea: Making, Sharing, Even Watching
item.description: In Korea, making a sexual deepfake of a real person is a crime even if never shared: up to 7 years or 50M won (Art. 14-2). Watching one: up to 3 years.

item.title: Threats in Korea (협박죄): Penalty, Texts and Dropping the Case
item.description: Threatening someone is 협박 in Korea: up to 3 years or 5M won (Criminal Act Art. 283), but no prosecution against the victim's wish. Not with a weapon.

item.title: Falsely Accused in Korea? False Accusation (무고죄) Explained
item.description: Filing a knowingly false report to get someone punished is 무고 in Korea: up to 10 years or 15M won (Criminal Act Art. 156). What to do if you're falsely accused.

item.title: Embezzlement in Korea (횡령): Penalties and How to Respond
item.description: Accused of embezzlement (횡령) in Korea? Up to 5 years, or 10 if it happened at work (Criminal Act Arts. 355-356). What counts and how to respond.

item.title: Collect a Debt in Korea Without a Hearing: Payment Order (지급명령)
item.description: Owed money in Korea? A payment order (지급명령) has no hearing: if the debtor does not object within 2 weeks of service, it works like a final judgment.

item.title: Trade Dispute With a Korean Company: Arbitration or Court?
item.description: Unpaid invoice or defective shipment from a Korean partner? A Korean attorney explains KCAB arbitration vs Korean courts, the CISG and freezing assets.

item.title: Re-entry Permit in Korea: Exempt for 1 Year, F-5 for 2 Years
item.description: Leaving Korea for a while? Most registered foreigners need no re-entry permit for 1 year (F-5: 2 years), but never past their period of stay. Check your card.

item.title: E-Scooter in Korea: Moped Licence Required or ₩100,000 Fine
item.description: Riding a rental e-scooter (전동킥보드) in Korea without a moped-class licence costs ₩100,000, no helmet ₩20,000. Riding drunk can cost your car licence too.

item.title: Obstruction of Business (업무방해) in Korea: Bar and Shop Disputes
item.description: A scene in a Korean bar or shop can be a minor offence or obstruction of business (업무방해), up to 5 years. A Korean attorney explains the line and your visa.

item.title: Hit a Taxi Driver in Korea? Why It Is Not Simple Assault
item.description: A shove in a taxi can be charged as assaulting a driver, an aggravated crime in Korea. A Korean attorney explains the penalties, settlement and your visa.

item.title: Employer Keeping Your Passport in Korea? It Is Illegal
item.description: Your employer in Korea keeps your passport or residence card "for safekeeping"? A Korean attorney explains why it is unlawful and how to get it back.

item.title: Gym or Pilates Refund in Korea: Cancel a Membership Early
item.description: Months left on a gym or pilates membership in Korea? A Korean attorney explains your right to cancel any time, the refund formula and what to do if refused.

item.title: Commercial Lease in Korea: Renewal, Rent Caps and Key Money
item.description: Opening a café, shop or office in Korea? A Korean attorney explains the commercial lease law: 10-year renewal, the 5% rent cap, key money and eviction.

item.title: Divorced Abroad, Still Married in Korea? Recording the Divorce
item.description: A divorce granted abroad does not update the Korean family register by itself. A Korean attorney explains recognition, the filing, and what still needs a court.

item.title: Scammed on a Secondhand App in Korea? What to Do Next
item.description: Paid for an item that never came? A Korean attorney explains what to do after a secondhand-trade scam in Korea: evidence, police report and getting money back.

item.title: Korean vs English Employment Contract: Which One Counts
item.description: Foreign employees in Korea often sign two versions of one contract. A Korean attorney explains which language governs and what to check before signing.

item.title: E-2 Visa Medical Check in Korea: Drug Test and Timing
item.description: A drug screen sits inside the routine E-2 medical check (채용신체검사). A Korean attorney explains what is tested, the timing and what a positive result means.

item.title: KIIP in Korea: What It Is Worth and Who Should Bother
item.description: KIIP (사회통합프로그램) shortens several immigration paths in Korea. A Korean attorney explains the levels, what completion replaces and who should actually bother.

item.title: Can Foreign Workers Join a Union in Korea?
item.description: Union rights in Korea attach to workers, not to visa status. A Korean attorney explains who may join, unfair labour practice and protection from retaliation.

item.title: Minimum Wage in Korea: What Foreign Workers Are Actually Owed
item.description: Korea's minimum wage applies to foreign workers on the same terms. A Korean attorney explains weekly holiday pay (주휴수당) and what may lawfully be deducted.

item.title: Working Outside Your Visa Category in Korea
item.description: A second job outside what your visa permits needs prior permission in Korea. A Korean attorney explains 체류자격외 활동허가 and the exposure for the employer.

item.title: Mandatory Child Abuse Reporting for Foreign Teachers in Korea
item.description: Foreign teachers and hagwon staff in Korea are mandatory reporters. A Korean attorney explains the duty, the fine for ignoring it, and good-faith protection.

item.title: Maternity and Parental Leave in Korea: Foreign Workers Qualify Too
item.description: Same rules as Korean staff: maternity leave (출산전후휴가), spousal leave and parental leave (육아휴직), paid through Employment Insurance. Who qualifies, how to ask.

item.title: Called In as a Witness in Korea
item.description: Korean police may call you in 'just as a reference'. A Korean attorney explains how a 참고인 becomes a 피의자 and what you may refuse to answer before going.

item.title: When Your Korean Employer Shuts Down or Stops Paying
item.description: Wages stop, the office empties, and your visa is tied to the company. A Korean attorney explains the wage guarantee fund and the immigration clock that starts.

item.title: Borrowed-Name Accounts in Korea: The Risk of Lending Your Name
item.description: A borrowed-name (차명) bank account, business or phone line in Korea: lending your name is often the offence itself. A Korean attorney explains the liability.

item.title: Buying a Used Car in Korea as a Foreigner
item.description: The inspection report is a legal document, and most disputes turn on it. A Korean attorney explains dealer versus private sale, the warranty and the transfer.
